name: two-step-view
intent: Split presentation into two transformations - first turn domain data into a channel-neutral logical page, then render that logical page into a concrete output format - so page structure is defined once while look-and-feel and output channel live entirely in the renderer.
problem: Every page owns its own presentation decisions: with one template or one transform per page, a global look-and-feel change means editing every file, and serving a second channel (print/PDF, e-mail, plain text, a machine-readable feed) means duplicating the page's structure. Nothing in the codebase represents 'the page' independently of the markup it currently happens to be rendered as.
context: Server-side presentation or document-publishing boundaries where several output channels share one page structure, or where the house style changes often enough that it must change in exactly one place. It also fits where the rendering technology is expected to be replaced (XSLT today, a template engine or PDF formatter tomorrow) and where the page should be inspectable, testable or cacheable before it is rendered.
benefits: Page structure is defined exactly once: every channel renders the same logical page, so a new channel adds a renderer instead of a copy of the page logic.

Global look-and-feel changes are local - restyling means editing one renderer or one stylesheet rather than every template, which is precisely the duplication Fowler cites against Template View and Transform View.
The logical page is a first-class, channel-neutral artefact: it can be asserted in tests, logged, diffed or cached without parsing markup.
Renderer specialists and domain code are decoupled: stylesheet or template authors work against the page vocabulary and never against the domain model.
The rendering technology is replaceable: XSLT can give way to a template engine or a PDF formatter as long as the logical page stays stable.
Channel-specific concerns stay in one place per channel - escaping, layout, output encoding and media type - which makes both audits and additions cheaper.
tradeoffs: Two transformations plus a retained intermediate raise CPU and peak memory roughly in proportion to the page, and buy nothing at all when only one channel exists.
The logical page is a second internal contract: it needs a vocabulary, a change rule and its own tests, and teams regularly under-invest until the 'logical' page quietly fills with HTML attributes.
Failures localise badly - a wrong byte can come from the page builder or from the renderer - and stylesheet-style renderers give far worse diagnostics than a debugger.
Renderer toolchains have real limits: XSLT 1.0 in libxslt and in .NET's XslCompiledTransform, XSLT 2.0/3.0 only through Saxon-style processors, plus scarce XSLT skills in most teams.
Renderers drift apart: nothing in the pattern stops one channel from omitting a field or formatting it differently, so every renderer needs a conformance fixture built from the same logical page.

participants.responsibility: Supplies the values the page must show; the page builder reads it and renderers never reach back into it.
Stage one: walks the domain data and produces the logical page - sections, elements and fields named in domain vocabulary, free of channel-specific markup.
The format-independent intermediate that every renderer consumes and that tests, caches and logs can inspect; the pattern's real contract.
Stage two: turns the logical page into exactly one channel's output (HTML, PDF, plain text, XML/JSON feed, e-mail) and owns all of that channel's formatting, encoding and escaping.
Decides which renderer serves a request or job - normally by content negotiation or an explicit route/format - and keeps that decision out of the page builder.
The concrete medium (browser HTML, print/PDF, e-mail body, machine-readable feed) whose constraints are expressed only inside its own renderer.

use_cases: Multi-channel publishing: one invoice or statement rendered as HTML for a portal, XSL-FO/PDF for print and plain text for e-mail from a single logical page.
Site-wide restyling in a CMS or portal where the house style must be one artefact to change and review rather than one edit per page family.
API-plus-HTML endpoints: the same logical page is serialised as JSON for clients and rendered as HTML for the browsable interface.
Document and report pipelines in the DocBook tradition: the logical document is produced once and rendered to HTML, PDF and e-book formats by different stylesheets.
Constrained or legacy channels - plain text, WAP/XML, CSV - added next to HTML without touching the page assembly code.
Pages produced once and consumed by several renderers or locales: the logical page is cached and rendered per channel on demand.

Spring Web MVC XSLT views: an XsltController builds an XML DOM of the page content, puts it in the model, and XsltViewResolver applies a home.xslt stylesheet - stage one produces the logical document, stage two owns the HTML.

Aura.View (PHP) ships the pattern under the name TwoStepView: a content template renders first, then a separately registered layout wraps it via setLayout()/getContent(), keeping the site chrome in one artefact instead of every page.

Standards-based publishing toolchains: the DITA Open Toolkit transforms semantic DITA maps/topics through XSLT stages into HTML, PDF and other deliverables, and Apache Cocoon pipelines generator -> XSLT transformer -> serializer so one XML source serves HTML, PDF, SVG and text.
avoid_when: Only one channel and one page family exist: a single Template View or Transform View is less machinery for the same result.
Pages share no structure at all, so there is no logical page worth defining and the intermediate becomes a pass-through with extra hops.
The output is inherently interactive and rendered client-side, where the channel-specific work happens in the browser and a server-side second stage adds nothing.
Latency or memory budgets forbid a second transformation and a retained tree (very large pages, streaming requirements) - render as you stream instead.
Nobody owns the page vocabulary: without a maintained definition the second stage degenerates into a thinner copy of the first.
anti_patterns: A 'logical' page that already contains HTML - div/span/class attributes in the intermediate make the renderer a formality and reopen the duplication the pattern exists to remove.
Renderers that pull from the domain layer or hit the database, hiding queries and lazy loading inside presentation.
One 'logical' page per channel, i.e. a page schema that changes with the output format - duplicated presentation under a new name.
Pre-escaping content in the page builder so every renderer inherits one channel's entities and the next renderer double-escapes.
An unversioned page schema treated as an untouchable public API, so the intermediate outlives the pages it was designed for.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: content and page structure belong to stage one, channel-specific formatting to stage two.
Open/closed principle: new output channels arrive as new renderers, without editing the page builder.
Information hiding: renderers see the logical page, never the domain model or the data source.
DRY: the page's structure has exactly one definition, which is the pattern's whole point.
Dependency direction: renderers depend on the page vocabulary; the vocabulary depends on nothing channel-specific.
best_practices: Define the logical page vocabulary (element names, required fields, allowed nesting) explicitly and treat changes to it as versioned contract changes.
Keep the page channel-neutral: domain vocabulary only, no markup attributes, no display formatting, no pre-escaped strings.
Escape and format inside the renderer - one renderer per channel - and prefer renderers with auto-escaping defaults.
Compile or parse renderers once and reuse them; create per-request renderer state only where the API demands it.
Test the logical page structurally and every renderer against the same fixture page, so drifting channels fail CI rather than production.
Never load a stylesheet or template from an untrusted source, and keep renderer escape hatches (XSLT scripting, document(), unsafe fragments) disabled unless deliberately enabled.
Cache or buffer the logical page when several channels or locales consume it, and log which renderer served a response.
sources: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) - Two Step View, chapter 14 (Web Presentation Patterns).
